How your tax is worked out

  1. Income under each head: salary (after the standard deduction, and HRA and professional tax in the old regime), house property, business, capital gains and other sources.
  2. Deductions come off income taxed at slab rates (most of them in the old regime only). They never reduce capital gains taxed at special rates.
  3. Slab income is taxed at the regime's slab rates; capital gains, crypto and winnings at their own flat rates. Residents whose slab income is below the exemption limit use the unused part against equity capital gains.
  4. The rebate, then surcharge with marginal relief, then the 4% cess.

Rebate, surcharge, cess and capital gains

  • Rebate. New regime: no tax if taxable income is up to ₹12 lakh (rebate up to ₹60,000), with relief just above it. Old regime: no tax up to ₹5 lakh (rebate up to ₹12,500). Residents only. In the new regime the rebate does not cover tax on capital gains at special rates.
  • Standard deduction. ₹75,000 in the new regime, ₹50,000 in the old, for salaried people and pensioners.
  • Surcharge. 10% of the tax above ₹50 lakh of income, 15% above ₹1 crore, 25% above ₹2 crore, and 37% above ₹5 crore in the old regime only (the new regime stops at 25%). On capital gains and dividends it never exceeds 15%. Marginal relief applies at each step.
  • Cess. 4% health and education cess on the tax and surcharge.
  • Capital gains. Equity funds and listed shares: 20% short term, 12.5% long term above ₹1.25 lakh a year. Other long-term gains: 12.5% without indexation. Debt funds bought from April 2023: your slab rate.

Rules last checked 25 Nov 2026, under the Income-tax Act, 2025. Deductions are shown by their familiar names (80C, 80D and so on); the new section numbers will be added from the tax department's official mapping.

Common questions

Which tax regime is better for me in FY 2026-27?

The new regime is lower for most people because of its wider slabs and the ₹12 lakh rebate. The old regime wins only with large deductions: at a ₹15 lakh salary, more than about ₹5.5 lakh beyond the standard deduction; at ₹25 lakh and above, about ₹8 lakh. The calculator compares both for your own numbers.

Is income up to ₹12 lakh tax-free?

In the new regime, yes, for residents with taxable income up to ₹12 lakh, through the rebate. For salaried people that means a salary up to ₹12.75 lakh after the ₹75,000 standard deduction. Capital gains taxed at special rates are not covered by the rebate.

What deductions are allowed in the new regime?

The standard deduction (₹75,000), your employer's NPS contribution (up to 14% of basic and DA), and deductions within house property for a let-out home. 80C, 80D, HRA and home-loan interest on a self-occupied home are not allowed.

Do senior citizens get a higher exemption?

Only in the old regime: ₹3 lakh at 60 to 79 and ₹5 lakh at 80 and above, for residents. The new regime has one set of slabs for every age. Seniors also get a ₹50,000 deduction for deposit interest under 80TTB and a ₹50,000 health insurance limit under 80D in the old regime.

How are NRIs taxed?

On income earned or received in India, at the same slabs. NRIs do not get the rebate, the higher exemption for seniors, 80TTB, or the use of the unused basic exemption against capital gains.

What changed with the Income-tax Act, 2025?

It replaced the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026. It keeps the rates and limits, renumbers the sections, and replaces the old 'previous year' and 'assessment year' with a single tax year: tax year 2026-27 is 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027, what used to be FY 2026-27 / AY 2027-28. Returns for it are due by 31 July 2027 for most individuals.

What is not included in this calculator?

Agricultural income, HUFs, firms and companies, alternative minimum tax, foreign tax credits, clubbing of income, set-off of brought-forward losses and some rare deductions. If any apply to you, have a CA check the result.

When is the last date to save tax for FY 2026-27?

31 March 2027 for investments and payments that count (80C, 80D, NPS). The return is due by 31 July 2027 for most individuals, and advance tax instalments fall on 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March.
